The phrase was understood as a description of a settled direction rather than a decree about a person who still intends to turn, and the difference between the two readings matters to anyone who fears for a relative. The verse describes the ones who have been fully described already in the passage, and it does not give the community a licence to write anyone off while he is alive. What follows is a longer picture that includes the same men in a storm, and the picture gives them movement even while their eyes remain closed.

**A MAN WHO NAILS HIS WINDOWS SHUT**

Think of a man who nails his windows shut against a noise he dislikes and then complains that the house has no air. The verse describes the same arrangement in the matter of hearing, and it treats the closed windows as his own work. These days the instruments are fed or starved by what a person chooses to read, watch and repeat, and the passage tells him what happens to equipment that is never used for the purpose it was given. Nobody is asked to despise the men in the picture, and the reader is asked instead to notice that their road began with small refusals which each looked reasonable at the time. A person who can trace the first of those refusals in his own record is in a better position than one who only recognises it in a stranger. The sūrah turns next to the second picture, which shows the same people caught in weather they cannot manage, and the change in the image is a change in the kind of danger that surrounds them.

---

## Verse 2:19

> Or ˹those caught in˺ a rainstorm from the sky with darkness, thunder, and lightning. They press their fingers into their ears at the sound of every thunder-clap for fear of death. And Allah encompasses the disbelievers ˹by His might˺

**THE SECOND PICTURE AND THE STORM IT SETS THEM IN**

The sūrah gives a second picture for the same people, and this one puts them in the middle of a night storm: ***“Or ˹those caught in˺ a rainstorm from the sky with darkness, thunder”***, ***“and lightning”***. The early teachers read the storm as the revelation itself, since the rain that gives life is a fitting image for the Book that came down, and they read the darkness, the thunder and the flash as the doubts, the warnings and the moments of clarity that accompany it. Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatādah are credited with readings of this kind, in which the rain is the Qur'an, the darkness is their confusion, and the thunderclaps are the commands and prohibitions that strike the ear. The picture is placed after the first one for a reason, since the man with the borrowed lantern has lost his light, while the people of this picture are still travelling through a storm that gives them light in flashes. Both are descriptions of the same disease at different stages, and the sūrah wants the reader to hold both.

**THE GESTURE OF THE FRIGHTENED TRAVELLERS**

The middle of the verse describes what the people in the storm do: ***“They press their fingers into their ears at the sound of every thunder-clap”***, ***“for fear of death.”***. The gesture is exact and it is not mocked anywhere in the sentence, which is worth noticing in a passage about pretenders. Ibn ʿAbbās described the men as stopping their ears against the sound that frightened them, and the Book records the same reaction elsewhere in the language of the people who refused what they heard. The reason the picture works is that it shows belief and fear existing together in the same person, which is the condition of the pretender exactly: he is close enough to the message to be shaken by it and far enough from it to hope it passes. The Book describes the thunder itself as a creature that praises its Lord, which means the storm that frightens them is doing the work of its Maker while they crouch in it: (13:13 — **“The thunder glorifies His praises, as do the angels in awe of Him”**).

**THE SENTENCE THAT CLOSES THE PICTURE**

The verse ends with a statement that stops the reader from thinking the men are out of reach: ***“And Allah encompasses the disbelievers ˹by His might˺”***. The wording describes a power that surrounds the people it deals with, and the sentence is placed after the account of their running and hiding. The Book describes the same surrounding elsewhere when it speaks about the flash of the cloud and the power behind it: (24:43 — **“The flash of the clouds' lightning nearly takes away eyesight”**). The early teachers read the closing as a warning to the men themselves rather than as a comfort to the community, since the hiding in the verse is useless against the One who sent the storm. What turns on the sentence is that fear is not the same as faith, and a person can be frightened by the truth for years without ever submitting to it. The next verse stays with the same travellers and shows what they do when the light appears, which is the most honest part of the whole description.

**A FIELD WITH A LAMP THAT FLASHES**

Think of a group crossing a field at night while a storm throws a flash of light every few minutes. Each flash shows the path ahead, and each one reveals how far off the track they had drifted when it was dark. The people of this picture walk in the flashes and stand still in the intervals, which is a portrait of a person who acts on the truth when it moves him and stops when the feeling passes. These days a reader may find the same pattern in his own week, since a reminder can produce a burst of effort and the following silence can produce nothing at all. The verse does not remove the storm and it does not promise that the storm will end soon; it shows the men in it, and the reader who recognises the description has been told where he is standing.

---

## Verse 2:20

> It is as if the lightning were about to snatch away their sight. Whenever lightning strikes, they walk in its light, but when darkness covers them, they stand still. Had Allah willed, He could have taken away their hearing and sight. Surely Allah is Most Capable of everything

**THE LIGHT THAT COMES AND GOES**

The verse continues the storm and turns to what the lightning does to the people caught in it: ***“It is as if the lightning were about to snatch away their sight”***. The wording describes a flash so strong that the men expect to lose their eyes with it, and the earliest authorities kept the comparison for the terror the revelation produced in the hearts of people who had set themselves against it. Ibn ʿAbbās is credited with the reading that the flash stands for the moments when the truth is shown plainly to the pretenders and the thunder for the warnings that follow, and the description of the eye as the thing nearly taken away belongs to the same picture. The Book uses the same image for the lightning in another sūrah where its effect is described in a single phrase: (24:43 — **“The flash of the clouds' lightning nearly takes away eyesight”**). The picture therefore joins the storm of the previous verse and carries it further, since the danger has moved from the ears to the eyes.

**THE TWO MOVEMENTS OF THE SAME PEOPLE**

The verse then records the two things the men do: ***“Whenever lightning strikes, they walk in its light, but when darkness covers them, they stand still”***. The sentence states the rhythm of a person who moves only when he is carried by an emotion and stops the moment it has gone, and the early teachers read the walking as the small amount of good such people do while the flash lasts. The Book draws the line between the people who walk in steady light and those who move in fits in another sūrah where the two groups are shown at the end of the road: (57:12 — **“with their light shining ahead of them and on their right”**). The contrast is exact, because the light of the believers is described as their own for the journey and shining before them, while the light of this passage comes in flashes that reveal and then vanish. What turns on the difference is the state of the lamp inside the man rather than the brightness of the weather around him.

**THE SENTENCE THAT NAMES WHAT COULD HAVE HAPPENED**

The verse closes with a statement about power that is aimed at the men in the picture: ***“Had Allah willed, He could have taken away their hearing and sight”***. The sentence names the two instruments and connects them to the same will that was behind the loss of the light, and it states the matter as a possibility that was not carried out. The Book uses the closing formula of the verse in another place where a great matter is described, and the wording there is worth placing beside it: (16:77 — **“Surely Allah is Most Capable of everything”**). The earliest teachers explained the verse as a reminder that the respite is itself a mercy, since the men had deserved the loss of the instruments in this life and were given time instead. That is the reason the sentence follows the account of their hiding, because the Book is telling them that the storm they are dodging could have finished the matter long before. The words that end it, ***“Surely Allah is Most Capable of everything”***, are the same words the Book uses when it describes the Hour arriving in the blink of an eye.

**A SAILOR WHO SAILS BY THE FLASHES**

Think of a sailor who steers only when a flash of lightning shows him the rocks, and who drops his hands from the wheel the moment the sky goes dark. He will hit the rocks in one of the intervals, and the reason is not the dark or the flash but his own refusal to hold a course. The verse describes this kind of sailor with the respect that comes from truthfulness, since it does not pretend that the flashes were useless: the men did walk, and the walking is recorded. These days a reader can find the same pattern in a life built around the high moments of a season and the flat weeks between them, and the sūrah offers no remedy here beyond the portrait itself. The long account of the pretenders ends with this verse, and the sūrah then turns to address the readers as a community of worshippers, which is the subject of the verses that follow.

---

## Verse 2:21

> O humanity! Worship your Lord, Who created you and those before you, so that you may become mindful ˹of Him˺

**AN ADDRESS TO EVERY HUMAN BEING**

The sūrah turns from its long account of the pretenders and speaks over their heads to the whole of humanity: ***“O humanity! Worship your Lord”***. The address is wider than the two groups described before it, and it reaches the readers of the Book in every generation along with the community that first heard it. ʿAlqamah and Mujāhid are credited with the observation that every address in the Book beginning with this phrase was revealed in Mecca, while every address beginning with "O you who believe" belongs to Madinah, which places this command among the earliest of the sūrah's sentences in order of revelation. Ibn ʿAbbās read the call as directed at the people of Mecca and also, in another report, at the people of the Scripture, and the two readings show how wide the door is meant to stand. The command is not addressed to a rank of scholars or to a nation with a claim on God; it is addressed to the species.

**WHAT THE WORD WORSHIP CARRIES HERE**

The command is followed by the word for worship, and Ibn ʿAbbās gave the reading that in the Book the word carries the sense of declaring God one and alone. That reading keeps the sentence from shrinking into ritual, since the first thing worship asks of a person is that he settle who God is. The Book states the purpose of the whole creation in the same terms in another sūrah, and the sentence there would fit here without a change: (51:56 — **“I did not create jinn and humans except to worship Me”**). The reasoning that joins the two verses is the difference between a servant who performs a duty and a creature who exists for a purpose, and the verse in this sūrah is asking for the second understanding. That is why the command is placed before the account of the gifts that follows, because the gifts are the evidence and the worship is the answer.

**THE ARGUMENT FROM THE GENERATIONS BEHIND HIM**

The verse attaches the command to the act that made the commanded possible: ***“Who created you and those before you”***. The argument moves from the person in front of the sentence to the generations who stood in the same place and passed away, and it leaves the hearer with a lineage of creatures who were all brought into being by the same hand. The Book puts the same argument in the form of a question in another sūrah: (52:35 — **“Or were they created by nothing, or are they ˹their own˺ creators”**). The reason the second half of the phrase matters is that a person can allow a claim for his own existence and no further, and the verse widens the claim to everything that came before him. The reader is shown a chain whose beginning he cannot see, and he is told that the One who made the chain is the One he is being called to serve.

**THE PURPOSE NAMED IN THE LAST WORDS**

The verse closes with the object of the command, and the wording is one of purpose: ***“so that you may become mindful ˹of Him˺”***. The devout scholars noticed the shape of the expression, since hope is not a quality that belongs to God in the way it belongs to a creature, and they explained it as a promise in the form of an aim, so that the servant knows what the command is intended to produce in him. The Book names the same quality as the fruit of worship in a hundred places, and the sūrah itself opened by naming the mindful as the people who would be guided. The point is that the command is not aimed at producing a performance but at forming a person, which is a difference worth keeping. The Book names the same quality as the mark of the people it addresses when it speaks to the believers in another sūrah: (3:102 — **“Be mindful of Allah in the way He deserves”**). Think of a teacher who sets an exercise not to fill an hour but to leave the student with a habit of mind; the command here works in the same way, and it can be repeated today for the same result in anyone who answers it.

---

## Verse 2:22

> ˹He is the One˺ Who has made the earth a place of settlement for you and the sky a canopy; and sends down rain from the sky, causing fruits to grow as a provision for you. So do not knowingly set up equals to Allah ˹in worship˺

**THE GIFTS THAT ANSWER THE COMMAND OF THE VERSE BEFORE**

The command to worship is followed by a list of what the Lord has already done, and the list opens with the One being named: ***“˹He is the One˺”***, ***“Who has made the earth a place”***, ***“of settlement”***, ***“for you and the sky a canopy”***. The first gift is a ground that carries the weight of a life, and the phrase describes a floor that was made fit for dwelling rather than left as a hazard. Ibn ʿAbbās and others explained the canopy as a roof over the earth, raised without pillars and guarded from falling, and the picture is one of a house rather than of a wilderness. The Book states the same pair of gifts in another sūrah with almost the same words, which shows that the reader is meant to hear the sentence as part of a settled description of God's dealing with the human being: (40:64 — **“It is Allah Who made the earth a place of settlement for you and the sky a canopy”**).

**THE PROVISION THAT COMES DOWN AND COMES OUT**

The list widens to the rain and to what it produces: ***“and sends down rain from the sky,”***, ***“causing fruits to grow”***, ***“as a provision for you.”***. The order of the sentence is the order of a person's dependence, since the water arrives before the fruit and the fruit arrives before the eater knows he will need it. The Book repeats the same chain elsewhere as a reminder of where the arrangement comes from: (14:32 — **“causing fruits to grow as a provision for you”**). The phrase about provision covers everything a person lives on, whether he earned it by work or received it without work, and the wording leaves the credit with the sender of the rain. That is why the sentence does not mention farmers or markets, because the arrangement is older than either of them and larger than both. What turns on the sentence for the reader is that a man may spend his life producing food and never once look past the market to the chain that brought it, and the verse makes the chain visible in a single line.

**THE WARNING AT THE END OF THE LIST**

The verse closes with a prohibition attached to all that came before it: ***“So do not knowingly set up equals”***, ***“to Allah ˹in worship˺”***. The word for knowledge in the middle of the sentence is doing real work, since it removes ignorance as an excuse and leaves the hearer with what he already knows. The Book uses the same charge in a question that puts the whole matter in one line: (41:9 — **“And how can you set up equals with Him?”**). The reason the prohibition is placed after the gifts rather than before them is that the gifts are the proof, and a person who has received a house, a roof and food from one hand cannot plead that he did not know whose the hand was. Ibn ʿAbbās read the closing as a warning to those who knew the truth about God's oneness and still gave a share of their worship to something else, and the sūrah keeps that reading in view in the verses that follow. What turns on the word for knowledge is that the excuse of a person who never heard does not survive it, since the reader of this verse has heard the argument and can no longer claim the benefit of the doubt.

**A CHILD WHO THANKS THE WELL FOR THE WATER**

Think of a child who is brought water from the well by his father and thanks the well for it. The gratitude is real and the direction is wrong, and the mistake costs nothing until the day someone asks the child who built the well. The verse makes the same correction with the whole of a human life, and it does it by naming the gifts before it names the error, which is the way a good teacher corrects a student. These days a person can live inside a system of provision so efficient that the sender disappears behind the machinery, and the passage asks him to look up from the machinery once. Nobody is asked to despise the means; the child is asked to know whose hands carried the water, and the knowledge is what the next verse puts to the test with a challenge that no rival of God has ever answered.

---

## Verse 2:23

> And if you are in doubt about what We have revealed to Our servant, then produce a sûrah like it and call your helpers other than Allah, if what you say is true

**THE CHALLENGE THAT ANSWERS THE DOUBT**

After naming the gifts, the sūrah turns to the message itself and answers a doubt with an invitation to test it: ***“And if you are in doubt about”***, ***“what We have revealed to Our servant,”***. The servant named here is the Prophet, and the title is worth noticing, because the Book calls him a servant at the moment it stakes everything on the revelation he carries. Ibn ʿAbbās and the earliest teachers read the doubt as belonging to the pretenders and to those who had heard the message and hesitated, and the verse does not treat the doubt as a crime in itself. The Book states the same invitation in two other sūrahs with the number of sūrahs they were asked to produce named in each, which shows that the challenge was repeated as the message was repeated. What turns on the wording is that the reader is not asked to swallow the claim; he is told to test it with the tools he already has.

**WHAT THEY WERE TOLD TO BRING**

The invitation is specific: ***“then produce a sûrah like it”***. The demand is not for a book or for a poem but for something of the same kind as the shortest unit of what had been revealed, which means the challenge stands within the reach of anyone with a language and a claim. The Book repeats the same demand in two places with the helpers and the honesty clause attached, and one of them shows exactly how much help the challengers were permitted to gather: (10:38 — **“Produce one sûrah like it then, and seek help from whoever you can—other than Allah—if what you say is true!”**). A later sūrah widens the field to include every human being and every jinn, which removes the excuse of a small tribe in a small country: (17:88 — **“they could not produce its equal, no matter how they supported each other”**). The reason the challenge is confined to a single unit is that the claim being tested is specific, and the test is meant to be answerable rather than impossible.

**THE HELPERS THEY WERE TOLD TO CALL**

The verse allows the doubters to bring support: ***“and call your helpers other than Allah”***, ***“if what you say is true”***. The last clause places the whole matter under the truthfulness of the people making the claim, and the Book uses the same clause at the end of the other two versions of the challenge. Ibn ʿAbbās is credited with reading the helpers as the deities the doubters called on for support, and others took them as the witnesses and the men of eloquence whose testimony they were relying on. The reason the verse does not forbid them to consult anyone outside God is that the point is already decided by the invitation, since no ally of theirs can supply what the challenge requires. A reader who has ever been challenged to match a piece of work knows the difference between an open test and a closed one, and this one is left open on purpose so that the failure cannot be blamed on the rules. The people who took up the challenge left no sūrah behind, and the silence has held for fourteen centuries, which is the answer the verse was waiting for when it named the clause.

**A CRAFTSMAN WHO DARES THE TOWN TO COPY HIS WORK**

Think of a potter who sets a bowl in the market and tells every potter in the town to make its match, offering to pay for the clay and to allow any tool they like. The offer would be pointless in a market where a hundred men could do the work, and it is decisive in one where none of them can. The verse makes the same offer with the message and with the whole of a community's talent, and the offer has been open ever since. These days the text is available to more readers and in more languages than at any point in its history, and the invitation stands where it stood, which is why the doubt of a modern reader is met with the same test as the doubt of the first hearer. A person who takes the challenge seriously will read the Book with the question in his hands rather than with a verdict already written, and the sūrah leaves him free to do exactly that.

---

## Verse 2:24

> But if you are unable to do so—and you will never be able to do so—then fear the Fire fuelled with people and stones, which is prepared for the disbelievers

**A VERDICT PRONOUNCED BEFORE THE ATTEMPT**

The sūrah completes the test with a statement that turns it into a verdict: ***“But if you are unable to do so”***, ***“and you will never be able to do so”***. The construction announces the outcome before the challengers have tried, and the scholars explain the shape of it in the same way they explained the earlier verse of purpose: a condition spoken by God is not an expression of uncertainty but a statement of what will happen. The challenge was put to the pagans, the Jews and the Christians together, which means the test was offered to every community in the region that had a claim to a revelation and a reason to doubt this one. The wording is a prophecy before it is anything else, and the history of the text since that day has kept it standing. That is why the sūrah moves straight from the test to the consequence, because a challenge that cannot be met has finished its work. A doubter may still hold his doubt, and the sentence has told him in advance that the doubt is not something the text will lose sleep over.

**THE FIRE THAT WAS MADE READY**

The consequence is named without decoration: ***“then fear the Fire fuelled with people”***, ***“and stones, which is prepared”***, ***“for the disbelievers”***. The verse describes the punishment as something standing ready rather than as something to be arranged later, and the wording about its fuel is exact. The early teachers read the people as the disbelievers themselves, and the stones either as the idols that were worshipped or as a material that burns far hotter than wood, which is how they explained the intensity of the fire. Ibn ʿAbbās is credited with the reading that the stones are the idols themselves, and the Book makes that reading explicit in another sūrah where the objects of worship are named as fuel beside the people who served them: (21:98 — **“you ˹disbelievers˺ and whatever you worship instead of Allah will be the fuel of Hell”**). The Book repeats the same phrase in a command to the believers a few sūrahs later, where they are told to shield their families from it: (66:6 — **“a Fire whose fuel is people and stones”**).

**WHY THE WARNING FOLLOWS THE CHALLENGE**

The order of the two verses is part of the argument, and the reason is worth stating plainly. The sūrah first offers the doubters a way of testing the message with their own abilities, then tells them that the test will not be passed, and then sends them to the consequence with their eyes open. A person who has been shown that the text is beyond him has no ground left for treating the matter as an opinion he may sample at leisure, because the claim he is dismissing has proved itself in the only arena he asked for. The Book uses the same sequence elsewhere when it challenges the doubters to bring ten sūrahs and then states the failure they will meet: (11:13 — **“Produce ten fabricated sûrahs like it and seek help from whoever you can—other than Allah—if what you say is true!”**). What turns on the sequence is that the warning is aimed at a person who has already been given his chance rather than at a stranger who never heard.

**A MAN WHO IGNORES A SIGNED WARNING**

Think of a traveller who reaches a bridge with a warning board signed by the engineer who built it, and who decides that the board is the opinion of an interested party. The bridge does not fail because he doubted it, and it does not wait for his book of reasons either. The verse treats the message in the same way, and it gives the reader the test first and the consequence afterwards, which is the fairest order the matter can have. These days a person may live inside a culture where every claim is treated as one option among many, and this verse asks him to notice that some claims have been tested in the way he would have chosen to test them. The next verse turns from the warning to the good news, and the sūrah shows that the same Book that leaves the doubter without an excuse gives the believer more than he asked for.

## Verse 2:187

> It has been made permissible for you to be intimate with your wives during the nights preceding the fast. Your spouses are a garment for you as you are for them. Allah knows that you were deceiving yourselves. So He has accepted your repentance and pardoned you. So now you may be intimate with them and seek what Allah has prescribed for you. ˹You may˺ eat and drink until you see the light of dawn breaking the darkness of night, then complete the fast until nightfall. Do not be intimate with your spouses while you are meditating in the mosques. These are the limits set by Allah, so do not exceed them. This is how Allah makes His revelations clear to people, so they may become mindful ˹of Him˺

## Verse 2:217

> They ask you ˹O Prophet˺ about fighting in the sacred months. Say, “Fighting during these months is a great sin. But hindering ˹others˺ from the Path of Allah, rejecting Him, and expelling the worshippers from the Sacred Mosque is ˹a˺ greater ˹sin˺ in the sight of Allah. For persecution is far worse than killing. And they will not stop fighting you until they turn you away from your faith—if they can. And whoever among you renounces their own faith and dies a disbeliever, their deeds will become void in this life and in the Hereafter. It is they who will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever.”

## Verse 2:233

> ˹Divorced˺ mothers will breastfeed their offspring for two whole years, for those who wish to complete the nursing ˹of their child˺. The child’s father will provide reasonable maintenance and clothing for the mother ˹during that period˺. No one will be charged with more than they can bear. No mother or father should be made to suffer for their child. The ˹father’s˺ heirs are under the same obligation. But if both sides decide—after mutual consultation and consent—to wean a child, then there is no blame on them. If you decide to have your children nursed by a wet-nurse, it is permissible as long as you pay fairly. Be mindful of Allah, and know that Allah is All-Seeing of what you do

> Or ˹are you not aware of˺ the one who passed by a city which was in ruins. ## Verse 2:282

> O believers! When you contract a loan for a fixed period of time, commit it to writing. Let the scribe maintain justice between the parties. The scribe should not refuse to write as Allah has taught them to write. They will write what the debtor dictates, bearing Allah in mind and not defrauding the debt. If the debtor is incompetent, weak, or unable to dictate, let their guardian dictate for them with justice. Call upon two of your men to witness. If two men cannot be found, then one man and two women of your choice will witness—so if one of the women forgets the other may remind her. The witnesses must not refuse when they are summoned. You must not be against writing ˹contracts˺ for a fixed period—whether the sum is small or great. This is more just ˹for you˺ in the sight of Allah, and more convenient to establish evidence and remove doubts. However, if you conduct an immediate transaction among yourselves, then there is no need for you to record it, but call upon witnesses when a deal is finalized. Let no harm come to the scribe or witnesses. If you do, then you have gravely exceeded ˹your limits˺. Be mindful of Allah, for Allah ˹is the One Who˺ teaches you. And Allah has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of all things

## Verse 2:286

> Allah does not require of any soul more than what it can afford. All good will be for its own benefit, and all evil will be to its own loss. ˹The believers pray,˺ “Our Lord! Do not punish us if we forget or make a mistake. Our Lord! Do not place a burden on us like the one you placed on those before us. Our Lord! Do not burden us with what we cannot bear. Pardon us, forgive us, and have mercy on us. You are our ˹only˺ Guardian. So grant us victory over the disbelieving people.”
